session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: Frame participants as men reflecting on their everyday lives — the places they go, the food they eat, the people they eat with. Speak from the position of someone genuinely curious about ordinary, specific experience, not abstract opinion. Keep the collective framing loose enough that each man can locate himself in it without feeling labelled.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): High risk of socially desirable or deflective answers ('gender doesn't really affect me'). Requires early behavioural grounding and willingness to surface contradictions between stated attitudes and described behaviours.

Plant-based shift and barriers (Section 4): Risk of rehearsed or politically safe answers about cost, taste, or convenience that mask deeper social and identity-based resistance. Need to push past the first layer of practical objections.

Social acceptability of masculine vs. plant-based foods (spans Sections 3–5): The group may converge quickly on safe, politically progressive positions while actually holding more nuanced or conflicted views. Consensus risk is significant here.

What would make plant-based more appealing (Section 5): Risk of abstract or generic suggestions ('better taste', 'lower price') rather than specific, personal accounts. Need to anchor in real social contexts already surfaced in earlier sections.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability on gender and food: All three participants are likely aware that 'gender doesn't affect my choices' is the acceptable answer. Plan to use behavioural grounding (specific past meals, specific social contexts) rather than direct attitude questions early in Section 3.

Premature consensus on plant-based barriers: The group may quickly settle on taste and cost as the main barriers, foreclosing exploration of identity and social acceptability. Plan a sharpening move or invite_dissent if this happens.

Rural–urban divergence: Mark's rural background may produce a genuinely different perspective, but he may also self-censor if the group dynamic feels urban-dominated. Watch for this and reactivate if needed.
Small group size (3 participants): With only three participants, if one becomes dominant the others may disengage quickly. Monitor balance more carefully than in a larger group.

Topic has a politically charged dimension (meat, masculinity, veganism): Participants may perform progressiveness, or alternatively perform resistance, rather than giving genuine accounts. Behavioural anchoring throughout is essential.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Hold back in intro and context sections — light touch, let participants establish their own framings and vocabulary. In Section 2 (everyday food decisions), begin gentle behavioural grounding to surface the real texture of their food lives. In Sections 3–5 (the main research territory), push harder: use direct probes when answers are vague, surface contradictions when they appear, invite dissent when consensus hardens too quickly. In the closing section, return to a lighter touch — a genuine open invitation rather than a deep probe. Overall: earn the right to push harder by building rapport early and staying genuinely curious throughout.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) carry the bulk of the research value and receive the heaviest word and turn allocation. Context sections (1, 2) are given moderate time — enough to build rapport and surface relevant behavioural texture that will feed into later sections, but not so much that they consume the session. Intro and closing are kept tight.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What’s your favourite place in your city to spend time with your male
friends? Why? Feel free to be specific.
How do you decide what to eat?
suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 5: Making plant-based foods more appealing
discussion_guide.scripted_question:
What might make plant-based foods more appealing to you or other men
you know?

Okay everyone, that’s our time. Thanks so much for participating
today. Before we finish, is there anything else you would like to add
about food choices, gender, masculinity, or plant-based eating?

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section deepened the earlier belonging-and-routine thread into a more precise phenomenological territory: the distinction between unconscious embeddedness in masculine norms versus conscious effort to maintain them. section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section pushed the earlier unconscious-embeddedness theme into a sharper moral register: the distinction between chosen comfort and involuntary loss. section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section converged on a shared structural conclusion from three distinct positions: plant-based appeal is not a food question but an infrastructure and normativity question. The convergence itself became the finding.

transcript.content: Hi everyone, really glad you could all make it today. So we've got about 45 minutes together, and this is going to be recorded just for research purposes — so if that's okay with you all, we'll get going. My name's Alex, and my job today is really just to keep things moving — I'm not here to steer you toward any particular answers, because honestly there aren't any right ones. What we're after is just your genuine experience and your genuine views, whatever those happen to be. So if something strikes you as obvious or boring or something you feel a bit conflicted about, all of that is useful. The main thing is to speak honestly rather than trying to give the 'correct' answer, because there really isn't one. And this is meant to be a conversation between you — so if something one of you says connects with your experience, or you see it differently, please just jump in. You don't need to wait for me to call on you. Okay — let's start simple. If you each want to say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today, that'd be great.
Right, yeah — I'm Mark, I'm from out in the countryside here, East of England. Not far from Norwich actually, proper rural bit. Been living out here for quite a few years now.

Great, thanks all. So we've got Gregor up in the North West, James down in the South East, and Mark out in rural East Anglia — good spread. Right, let's get into it. I want to start with something fairly easy — thinking about the places you spend time with your male friends. Is there a particular spot, a favourite place, that comes to mind? Could be a pub, a park, someone's house, wherever — somewhere you genuinely like going with your mates. What is it, and what makes it the one?

Yeah, good question. For me it's probably the pub down the road, the White Hart actually. Nothing fancy about it, but that's kind of the point. It's been there forever, same landlord for years, and you get a decent mix of people in there — not just younger lads, you know? It's got a bit of atmosphere without being loud or trying too hard. We'll usually go in there maybe once a week, couple of us, sometimes more. 

What I like about it is you can actually have a conversation. The telly's on but it's not blaring at you, and you're not fighting to hear each other like you would in some of these trendy places. And the landlord knows us, so there's that familiarity. Plus the beer's decent and not overpriced, which matters when you're going regularly.

It's not like we're doing anything special when we go — it's just comfortable, I suppose. We talk about work, football sometimes, just whatever's going on. Doesn't need to be anything more than that.

Yeah, well that sounds nice and all, but I'll be honest — I don't really have that anymore. I mean, I've got places I go, but it's not the same as what you're describing. There used to be a couple of good pubs round here, proper local spots where you'd just drop in, you know? But a lot of them have shut down over the last few years. It's just changed.

There's still one I'll go to now and again with a couple of lads, but it's... I dunno, it feels different. Either the landlord's changed or it's trying to be something it's not, or it's just quieter because half the regulars have moved on or stopped going out as much. And some of the others have turned into these sort of gastropubs or whatever, all craft beer and fancy food, which is fine if that's your thing but it's not really a place to just be, is it?

That thing you said about not doing anything special — that's exactly what I miss. You don't need to plan an evening or dress up for it. You just went in, had a pint, had a chat. Took it for granted really at the time, but once it's gone you realize what you've lost. So yeah, I don't really have that equivalent anymore, if I'm honest.

Yeah, that's it exactly. You're right — you do take it for granted. I mean, I've still got the White Hart, so I'm lucky in that sense, but even round here you see it happening. There's a couple of pubs that have closed in the last five or six years, places people used to go. And like you say, the ones that are left sometimes try to rebrand themselves into something completely different. More profit margins maybe, but it doesn't feel like a pub anymore.

It's a shame because it's not really replaceable, is it? You can't just go somewhere else and get the same thing. It's about the routine of it, the people you see regularly. When those places disappear, something shifts. You can't just pop in the same way anymore.

I think that's what made the White Hart work for me — it's stayed kind of... stable. Hasn't tried to become a wine bar or whatever. But I'm aware that could change any time. You hear about different chains moving in, or property developers wanting the land. It feels more precarious than it used to be, if that makes sense.

Right, yeah — and that's the thing, isn't it? You can see it coming sometimes. You notice the place getting a bit quieter, fewer of the old faces, and you think, how long's this going to last? It's not even about the landlord changing their mind necessarily. It's just economics, innit. These places don't make money the way they used to.

But what gets me is it's happening now. Like, I'm not worrying about some future threat — I'm already living through it. I've already lost two or three spots I used to go to regularly. They're just gone. And it's not like there's some plan to fix it or bring them back. They're either boarded up or they've become something else entirely.

The worst part is there's no alternative that feels the same. You can go somewhere else, yeah, but it's not the same people, it's not the same routine. You lose that without really having chosen to lose it, if you know what I mean? It's just being taken away bit by bit.

And I suppose the thing that bothers me about it is — I'm not even that young anymore, I'm 53 — but I can see what's left shrinking. So what's it going to be like in another ten years? Where are you supposed to go and just... be, without it being some sort of experience or night out you've got to plan for?

I hear you, Gregor. That's a real thing, what you're describing. And you're right — it's not some distant worry for you, it's already happened. That's different from me sitting here thinking it might happen.

I suppose the difference is I've still got mine, but I'm under no illusions about how long that lasts. Could change tomorrow, couldn't it? New owner, new direction, and suddenly it's something else. You lose that without having any say in it, like you said. It's just gone.

What gets me about it too is there's no real replacement for it. You can find another pub, sure, but you're starting from scratch again. You've lost the people, the routine, the familiarity. It takes years to build that up, and then it just disappears. And then you're supposed to just find somewhere else and do it all again? At our age?

I think what you're saying about the next ten years — I'm fifty, so I'm not that far off where you are — and yeah, that does make you think. How many of these places are actually going to survive? It feels like they're becoming fewer. And the ones that do might not be the kind where you can just drop in and be comfortable without it being a whole production.
Mark, you've been listening to all of this — where does it land for you coming from rural East Anglia?

Yeah, well... it's a bit different out where I am, I think. I mean, I get what you're both saying about the pubs closing down — that's happening here too, no question about it. But out in the villages, there's fewer of them to start with, so when one goes it feels like a bigger deal somehow.

I don't really have a regular spot the way you're describing, James. There's a couple of pubs within driving distance, but they're not... I mean, I'll go occasionally, but it's not like I'm popping in regularly with a group of mates or anything. That's just not how it works out here. Most people I know, if they're going out, they're driving somewhere a bit bigger — into town or whatever — rather than having a local.

For me it's more... I see my mates, but it's often at someone's house, or we'll go fishing, something like that. Less about having a fixed place, more about just arranging something when it suits. Which is fine, but I suppose what you're both touching on — that thing about just being able to turn up somewhere and know it'll be there, the same people, the same routine — I don't think I've ever really had that, not in the same way.

But I do understand what you mean about something disappearing without you choosing it. That's a different feeling, isn't it?

Thanks Mark — that's a real contrast, isn't it, that thing of never quite having the fixed local to lose in the first place. Okay, let's move on a bit. Sticking with the everyday stuff — how do you actually decide what to eat? Like, on a normal day, what's shaping that?
So thinking about a typical week — how do you actually decide what to eat? Not the ideal version, just what actually happens.

Yeah, but hang on — I think Mark's making a good point there that's almost the opposite of what he's saying. I mean, he's never had that fixed spot, right? So he's never lost it either. But what James and I are talking about — we did have it, and now it's gone. That's different.

And I'm not sure just jumping to food choices captures what we're actually on about here. It's not really about the pub as a place to eat, is it? It's about having somewhere you belong without thinking about it. Without it being a choice you have to make.

Mark said something quite sad there, actually — that he's never really had that routine. And for us, we're losing it. So we're in different boats, but both of us are sort of... without that thing, at the end of it.

I'm not saying this to be difficult, but it feels like we're in the middle of saying something that matters, and then suddenly we're talking about what's for tea. Which is fine, but it's a bit of a shift, you know?

Gregor, I take that — there was something real in what you were all getting at, and I don't want to brush past it. But I think it actually connects to what I want to ask now. You were talking about having somewhere you belong without it being a choice you have to make. That sense of routine, of something just being there — I'm curious whether food works a bit like that for any of you too. Not the pub specifically, but the day-to-day: do you find yourselves making food choices, or do they just kind of... happen?

Yeah, that's fair what you said, Gregor. I wasn't trying to brush it off — you're right, there's something different about losing something versus never having it in the first place.

But now you mention it, with the food thing — I think I do have a bit of that, actually. Not in the same way, maybe, but... I mean, most days I know roughly what I'm going to eat. Not consciously deciding it every morning, just sort of... it happens. There's certain things I'll make, routines around it. My wife knows what we're doing most nights without having to discuss it much.

There's probably three or four meals we rotate through, and we just do them. Monday's often a casserole or something slow, because of how the week works out. Weekends we might do something different. But it's not like I'm standing in front of the fridge thinking what shall I have — that's not really my style anyway.

I suppose what you're saying about belonging without choosing it — maybe that's a bit like it, yeah. You don't have to think about it. It's just there, it's familiar, it works. You're not trying to make it into something it's not.

Though I'm not sure that's quite the same as what you've lost with the pub, if I'm honest. It's a different kind of thing.

No, but... yeah, maybe you're onto something there. I mean, you're right it's not the same thing, but what you're saying about not having to think about it — that's exactly it, isn't it? That's what matters.

I hadn't thought about it that way before, but you're right. With the pub, you just went. You didn't have to decide. It was automatic. And what you're describing with the food — same thing. You don't have to think about Monday casserole, it just happens. That's the comfort of it.

The difference is you've still got your casseroles. They're not going anywhere. But yeah, now that you mention it, I suppose that routine thing — that's what you miss when it's gone. It's not even about the pub particularly, it's about having things that are just... settled. Predictable.

I mean, I still eat the same things most nights, I suppose. But it's different without the other thing. Without the pub being there to go to. It's like one habit was built on top of the other, you know? You'd go to the pub on a Thursday, that was your Thursday night sorted. And now that's just... not there.

So maybe what's disappeared is the bigger pattern of it. Not just one routine, but how all these routines fit together to make up your week, your life. That's harder to replace than just finding another casserole recipe.
